    Math 10A — Structure and Concepts in Math I

    §6.2

    Comparing Fractions

    Five strategies for comparing fractions, and the denseness of rational numbers

    §6.2 Today's Goal

    MATH 10A

    Today's Goal

    After completing this section, you should be able to:

    • Compare two fractions using common denominators, common numerators, missing parts, a benchmark number, or more larger parts versus fewer smaller parts, and choose an efficient strategy for a given pair
    • Test a conjecture about comparing fractions against the strategies above
    • Find a rational number between any two given rational numbers

    §6.2 Learning Target

    MATH 10A

    Learning Target 14

    LT.14 Comparing Fractions

    I can apply multiple strategies for comparing fractions.

    §6.2 Talk It Over

    MATH 10A

    Which Is Larger?

    Which is larger, 38 or 58? Why?

    Both fractions have the same denominator, so the whole is divided into the same number of equal parts. 38 is 3 one-eighths and 58 is 5 one-eighths.

    The units are the same and 5 is more than 3, so 58>38.

    §6.2 Common Denominators

    MATH 10A

    Common Denominators

    Procedure 6.2.2 Comparing Fractions Using Common Denominators

    To compare two fractions using common denominators, do the following.

    1. If the two fractions do not have common denominators, then rewrite them as equivalent fractions with the same denominator.
    2. Whichever fraction has the larger numerator is the larger fraction.

    For example, 4 one-fifths is more than 2 one-fifths because the units (i.e., one-fifth) are the same and 4 is more than 2.

    §6.2 Example 1

    MATH 10A

    Compare Using Common Denominators

    Use common denominators to compare each pair of fractions to determine which is larger.

    (a) 38 and 58

    Same denominator and 3<5.

    So 38<58.

    (b) 34 and 712

    34=3⋅34⋅3=912

    9>7, so 912>712.

    So 34>712.

    (c) 23 and 35

    The denominators 3 and 5 have a least common multiple of 15.

    23=2⋅53⋅5=1015

    35=3⋅35⋅3=915

    10>9, so 1015>915.

    So 23>35.

    §6.2 Common Numerators

    MATH 10A

    Common Numerators

    Procedure 6.2.5 Comparing Fractions Using Common Numerators

    To compare two fractions using common numerators, do the following.

    1. If the two fractions do not have the same numerator, then rewrite them as equivalent fractions with the same numerator.
    2. Whichever fraction has the larger denominator is the smaller fraction.

    38 is 3 one-eighths and 34 is 3 one-fourths. The unit fraction one-eighth is smaller than the unit fraction one-fourth.

    §6.2 Example 2

    MATH 10A

    Compare Using Common Numerators

    Use common numerators to compare each pair of fractions to determine which is larger.

    (a) 35 and 38

    Same numerator and 8>5.

    So 38<35.

    (b) 34 and 611

    34=3⋅24⋅2=68

    8<11, so 68>611.

    So 34>611.

    (c) 37 and 25

    The numerators 3 and 2 have a least common multiple of 6.

    37=3⋅27⋅2=614

    25=2⋅35⋅3=615

    14<15, so 614>615.

    So 37>25.

    §6.2 Missing Parts

    MATH 10A

    Missing Parts

    Procedure 6.2.8 Comparing Fractions Using Missing Parts

    To compare two fractions using missing parts, do the following.

    1. Determine what each fraction is missing to make one whole.
    2. Whichever fraction is missing more is the smaller fraction.

    This strategy is useful when fractions are close to one whole and the missing parts are easier to compare than the original fractions.

    §6.2 Example 3

    MATH 10A

    Compare Using Missing Parts

    Use missing parts to compare each pair of fractions to determine which is larger.

    (a) 56 and 67

    56 is missing 16 to make a whole.

    67 is missing 17 to make a whole.

    Since 16>17, we know that 56 is missing more than 67 is missing.

    So 56<67.

    (b) 58 and 710

    58 is missing 38 to make a whole.

    710 is missing 310 to make a whole.

    Since 38>310 (we get this by using the common numerator strategy), we know that 58 is missing more than 710 is missing.

    So 58<710.

    §6.2 Benchmark Numbers

    MATH 10A

    Comparing to Benchmark Numbers

    In some cases, we can compare the two fractions to another fraction, which we call a benchmark number. If one of the fractions is smaller than the benchmark number and the other fraction is larger than the benchmark number, then we know which of the two fractions is larger.

    For example, 38 is smaller than 12 and 56 is larger than 12. So 38<56.

    This strategy is useful when an appropriate benchmark number is easily identified.

    §6.2 Example 4

    MATH 10A

    Compare Using a Benchmark Number

    Use a benchmark number to compare 1316 and 712 to determine which is larger.

    Note that half of 16 is 8 and half of 12 is 6. This tells us that 1316 and 712 are both larger than 12. So 12 cannot be used as a benchmark number to help us.

    Instead, we will use 34 as our benchmark number. We can write 34 as equivalent fractions 1216=912.

    Since 1316>1216 and 712<912, we now know that 1316>712.

    §6.2 More Larger Parts vs Fewer Smaller Parts

    MATH 10A

    Our Last Strategy

    Our last strategy is the most straightforward one. If one fraction has a larger unit fraction than the other (i.e., its equal parts are larger) and that same fraction has more parts than the other fraction, then that fraction must be larger.

    For example, suppose we are comparing 37 and 45. Note that the unit fraction for 37 is one-seventh and the unit fraction for 45 is one-fifth. So 45 has the larger unit fraction. 45 also has more parts than 37 (4>3). Therefore, 45>37.

    This makes sense if you think about comparing distances. 4 miles is larger than 3 feet because miles are larger units than feet and we have more miles than we have feet.

    §6.2 More Larger Parts vs Fewer Smaller Parts

    MATH 10A

    Who Wins?

    §6.2 Example 5

    MATH 10A

    Compare Using More Larger Parts

    Use the “more larger parts vs fewer smaller parts” strategy to compare 47 and 29.

    The unit fraction for 47 is one-seventh and the unit fraction for 29 is one-ninth. So 47 has the larger unit fraction (i.e., larger parts).

    47 also has more parts than 29 (4>2). So 47>29.

    §6.2 Group Work

    MATH 10A

    Choose an Efficient Strategy

    Work with your group. For each pair, choose an efficient strategy, then decide which fraction is larger.

    (a) 910 and 1112 (b) 38 and 47 (c) 59 and 512

    The five strategies:

    • common denominators
    • common numerators
    • missing parts
    • comparing to benchmark numbers
    • more larger parts vs fewer smaller parts

    §6.2 Group Work, continued

    MATH 10A

    Which Strategy Did You Pick?

    Which strategy did your group pick? Did another group pick a different one?

    (a) Missing parts. 910 is missing 110 and 1112 is missing 112. Since 110>112, 910<1112.

    (b) Benchmark number 12. 38<12 and 47>12, so 38<47. More larger parts vs fewer smaller parts also works: one-seventh is larger than one-eighth, and 4>3.

    (c) Common numerators. Same numerator and 12>9, so 512<59.

    §6.2 Denseness

    MATH 10A

    The Denseness of Rational Numbers

    The rational numbers have a special property that is not true of the integers.

    Theorem 6.2.14 Denseness Property of Rational Numbers

    Given any two rational numbers ab and cd, there is another rational number between these two numbers.

    Notice that for integers, this doesn't work. For example, there is no integer between 4 and 5.

    §6.2 Example 6

    MATH 10A

    Find a Rational Number

    Find a rational number between 23 and 34.

    Rewrite each fraction with the same denominator of 12: 23=2⋅43⋅4=812 and 34=3⋅34⋅3=912.

    There isn't enough space between 812 and 912 to fit in another one-twelfth. So we will rewrite each fraction again with a larger common denominator of 24.

    23=2⋅83⋅8=1624 and 34=3⋅64⋅6=1824.

    Now, we can easily choose 1724 and be confident that it is between 23 and 34.
